Epaenetus
ee-PEE-nuh-tus
proper noun
From the Greek Epainetos, “praised” or “worthy of praise,” from epaineo, to commend.

Biblical Definition

Epaenetus is a believer at Rome whom the apostle Paul greets with peculiar warmth: “Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ” (Rom 16:5). Two marks of honour rest upon him. First, he was Paul’s wellbeloved, a man dear to the apostle’s heart, knit to him in the bond of the gospel. Second, and greater, he was “the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ,” among the earliest in that region to be brought from darkness to light and laid as a first sheaf upon the altar of God. The figure is drawn from the law, where the firstfruits of the harvest were offered to the Lord as a pledge of the whole crop to follow (Lev 23:10). So Epaenetus, an early convert, was a token and earnest of the great harvest the gospel would reap. Of his after-life Scripture tells us nothing; he is a name, a love, and a firstfruit, and no more. Yet that is enough. The Spirit set down his name forever as one whom Christ claimed early and Paul loved dearly. He stands for every believer who, brought first out of a household or a region, becomes a pledge that God has more people there, and a standing encouragement to labour on where one soul has already been won.

Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome, Paul’s wellbeloved, called the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ in Romans 16.

expand to see more

EPAENETUS, a Christian at Rome greeted by the apostle Paul.

Called Paul’s “wellbeloved,” a man dear to the apostle (Rom 16:5).

Named “the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ,” an early convert.

His Greek name signifies “praised” or “worthy of praise.”

Scripture records nothing of his life beyond the greeting.

Key Scripture

Rom 16:5 — "Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ."

1Co 16:15 — "I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)"

Rom 8:23 — "And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body."

Jas 1:18 — "Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures."

Modern Corruption

The honour of the early convert, a firstfruit and pledge of the harvest God will reap.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Epaenetus is the worth of the firstfruit. An early convert, laid as a first sheaf upon the altar, he was a pledge that God had a great harvest yet to gather where he had been the first to believe.

The firstfruit teaches patience and hope to those who labour for souls. One conversion is no small thing; it is an earnest of more, a token that the Lord is at work in a place. Epaenetus, Paul’s wellbeloved, reminds us that the Saviour claims men one by one, and that the first to come stands as a promise of the multitude that shall follow.

Hebrew Roots

A Greek personal name meaning “praised,” from the verb to commend or extol.

expand to see more

Epaenetus — Greek Epainetos, “praised” or “worthy of praise.”

From epaineo, to praise or commend.

Borne by an early convert of Achaia greeted at Rome.

The term firstfruits joined to him is drawn from the Levitical offering.

Scripture preserves the name only in Romans 16:5.

Usage

"Paul saluted Epaenetus, his wellbeloved and the firstfruits of Achaia."

"Like Epaenetus, the first convert of a place is a pledge of more to come."

"Epaenetus was laid as a first sheaf of the harvest unto Christ."
